mainTopic: The source and the detailed rules of a פועל's right to eat from the produce he works with
overview: The amud opens with the last words of the משנה, which lists the cases where a פועל (hired worker) may not eat from the produce he works with. The גמרא then asks where the worker's right to eat comes from. It tries to learn all crops from the פסוק about a כרם, and then from the פסוק about קמה. Each one turns out to have something special: עוללות for the vineyard and חלה for grain. A הצד השוה of the two is then attacked, because both are used on the מזבח. So שמואל learns the rule from the word חרמש, and רבי יצחק adds the word קמה to include all standing produce. The גמרא then asks why the כרם פסוק is needed at all. רבא answers that it teaches its own details, and a ברייתא lists them: it speaks of a worker, a Jew's vineyard (or, for one view, not הקדש), real eating of grapes alone, an exemption from מעשר like the owner, eating until full but not too much, and eating only while filling the owner's vessels. The amud ends as רבי ינאי begins a teaching about when טבל becomes obligated in מעשר, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the משנה: Cases Where a Worker May Not Eat
steps.stepSummary: The משנה finishes its list of cases where a פועל may not eat: produce still growing, produce already finished and detached, and things that do not grow from the ground.
steps.simpleTranslation: A worker may not eat when the produce is not at the stage of finishing its work, when it is detached from the ground after its work is already done, or when it is something that does not grow from the ground.
steps.whatsHappening: These are the final words of the משנה, finishing a list of workers who are NOT allowed to eat from the produce they work with.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives three cases where the worker loses his right to eat. In the first, the produce is still growing and not ready. In the second, it is already fully processed after harvest. In the third, it does not grow from the ground at all. Together these show the right to eat applies only to things that grow from the ground, at the moment their work is being finished.

keyTerms.meaning: The completion of the work, meaning the final stage, like harvesting
Detached, picked from the ground
Its growth is from the land
A hired worker

steps.confusionAlert: "בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאֵין גְּמַר מְלָאכָה" does not mean the worker is resting. It means the produce is still growing and not yet ready to be harvested.
steps.whyThisMatters: These three conditions are exactly what the גמרא will now try to find a source for: produce that grows from the ground, at the time its work is finished.

phrases.english: at a time that is not the completion of the work,
and with produce detached from the ground
after its work has already been completed,
and with something whose growth is not from the land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Conclusion of the משנה, which began on the previous daf
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A worker may not eat from produce that is still growing, that is detached and already fully processed, or that does not grow from the ground.

steps.title: Where Does the Worker's Right to Eat Come From?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by asking for the source of the rule that a worker may eat from the produce he is working with.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: From where do we know these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and asks where in the תורה we learn that a worker may eat while he works. This sets up the next step, where a פסוק is brought.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה stated the rule of a worker eating as if it were obvious. The גמרא wants a written source in the תורה behind it.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know these things? A standard request for a source

phrases.english: GEMARA: From where are these matters derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the משנה's rule
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source in the תורה that a worker may eat from the produce he works with

steps.title: The Source: The Verse About a Vineyard
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers with the פסוק that permits someone who enters his neighbor's כרם to eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: "When you come into your neighbor's vineyard, you may eat."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by quoting the פסוק that says someone working in another person's vineyard may eat the grapes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק talks about "coming into" a neighbor's כרם, which חז"ל understand as coming in to work as a hired worker. So the right to eat comes straight from this פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: Vineyard
Your neighbor, here meaning the owner you work for

phrases.english: As it is written:
"When you come into your neighbor's vineyard, then you may eat."
phrases.notes: דברים 23:25

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב: כִּי תָבֹא בְּכֶרֶם רֵעֶךָ וְאָכַלְתָּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the request for a source
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק "כִּי תָבֹא בְּכֶרֶם רֵעֶךָ וְאָכַלְתָּ" is the source.

steps.title: The Verse Only Mentions a Vineyard. What About Other Crops?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out that the פסוק only speaks about a כרם and asks how we know the rule applies to all produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have found a source for a vineyard. From where do we know it for everything else?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says the פסוק only covers a vineyard and asks how we know a worker may eat from other crops too. This sets up an attempt to extend the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה treats the worker's right as general, covering any crop that grows from the ground. The פסוק only names a כרם, so the גמרא needs a way to widen it.

keyTerms.meaning: We have found
All other things

phrases.english: We have found a source for a vineyard;
for all other things, from where do we know it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַשְׁכְּחַן כֶּרֶם, כֹּל מִילֵּי מְנָא לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Points out that the source in step 3 is too narrow
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source showing that the worker's right to eat applies to all crops, not just a vineyard

steps.title: Learning All Crops From the Vineyard
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא learns from כרם that any produce that grows from the ground, at the time its work is finished, may be eaten by the worker.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learn it from a vineyard. A vineyard is special in that it grows from the ground, and the worker eats from it at the time its work is being finished. So too, with anything that grows from the ground, at the time its work is being finished, a worker may eat from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by comparing all crops to a vineyard. Whatever shares the vineyard's key features gets the same rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא picks out two features of a כרם: it grows from the ground, and the worker eats at the time the work is finished. Any crop with both features is treated the same way. These two features match the conditions in the משנה (step 1).

keyTerms.meaning: We learn it out, we derive it
Just as X is special in this way, so too: a method of comparing cases by shared features
Things that grow from the ground

phrases.english: We derive it from a vineyard:
Just as a vineyard is special,
in that it is something that grows from the ground,
and at the time of the completion of its work
a worker eats from it,
so too, anything that grows from the ground,
at the time of the completion of its work,
a worker may eat from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4 by extending the vineyard rule
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: By a comparison to כרם: anything that grows from the ground, at the time its work is finished, may be eaten by the worker.

steps.title: A Vineyard Is Different Because of עוללות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the comparison: a כרם has a special obligation of עוללות, so other crops may not be like it.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about a vineyard? It is special, because it is obligated in עוללות!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the comparison from step 5 by pointing out a unique feature of a vineyard that other crops do not have.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A comparison only works if the source case has nothing special that could explain its rule. A כרם has the special מצוה of עוללות. Maybe that is why a worker may eat there, and other crops, which lack עוללות, would not get the same rule.

keyTerms.meaning: What about X? It is special because...: a standard way to break a comparison
Small, incomplete grape clusters that must be left for the poor

phrases.english: What about a vineyard?
It is special, because it is obligated in olelot!
phrases.notes: עוללות are small, incomplete grape clusters the owner leaves for the poor (ויקרא 19:10).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the comparison made in step 5
steps.kashyaTarget: The comparison of all crops to כרם
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A כרם has a unique feature (עוללות) that other crops lack, so its rule may not carry over to them.

steps.title: Learn Instead From Standing Grain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא switches its source: we learn the rule for all crops from קמה (standing grain) instead of from כרם.
steps.simpleTranslation: We derive it from standing grain.
steps.whatsHappening: Instead of defending the vineyard comparison, the גמרא picks a different source to learn from: standing grain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Grain does not have the מצוה of עוללות, so the challenge of step 6 does not apply to it. By learning from קמה, the גמרא avoids the problem completely.

keyTerms.meaning: Standing grain, still attached in the field

phrases.english: We derive it from standing grain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6 by switching the source case
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replaces the source case with a different one that lacks the problem
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All crops are learned from כרם, but כרם is special because of עוללות.
steps.terutzMaskana: All crops are learned from קמה, which has no עוללות.

steps.title: Where Do We Learn Standing Grain Itself?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that a worker may eat from קמה in the first place.
steps.simpleTranslation: Standing grain itself: from where do we know it?
steps.whatsHappening: Before we can learn other crops from standing grain, the גמרא asks how we know a worker may eat standing grain at all. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You can only learn from a case if that case itself has a clear source. So the גמרא checks that the rule for קמה is written in the תורה.

keyTerms.meaning: Itself

phrases.english: Standing grain itself, from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the new base case introduced in step 7
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that a worker may eat from standing grain

steps.title: The Verse About Standing Grain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the פסוק that allows someone who comes into his neighbor's קמה to pluck ears of grain with his hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is written: "When you come into your neighbor's standing grain, you may pluck ears with your hand."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק that directly permits eating from a neighbor's standing grain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just like the vineyard, standing grain has its own פסוק. So קמה is a solid base case, and the rule for all other crops can now be learned from it instead of from כרם.

keyTerms.meaning: And you may pluck
Ears of grain

steps.whatToRemember: The worker's right to eat is written in the תורה for כרם and for קמה. The גמרא tried to learn all crops from כרם, but כרם is special because of עוללות, so it switched to learning from קמה.

phrases.english: As it is written:
"When you come into your neighbor's standing grain,
phrases.notes: דברים 23:26

phrases.english: then you may pluck ears with your hand."

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּכְתִיב: כִּי תָבֹא בְּקָמַת רֵעֶךָ וְקָטַפְתָּ מְלִילוֹת בְּיָדֶךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק "כִּי תָבֹא בְּקָמַת רֵעֶךָ וְקָטַפְתָּ מְלִילוֹת בְּיָדֶךָ" is the source for קמה.

steps.title: Grain is special because of חלה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges learning all crops from קמה, since grain carries the מצוה of חלה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about standing grain? It is special because it is obligated in חלה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the new source from step 7. Maybe grain is special, so we cannot learn other crops from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same kind of attack the גמרא made against כרם in step 6. Dough made from grain needs חלה taken off, which most other produce does not need. Because of that special feature, maybe only grain gives a worker the right to eat.

keyTerms.meaning: Standing grain still in the field
The portion of dough given to a כהן; only applies to the five grains
'What about X, since it has...' — a formula for pointing out what makes a case special

phrases.english: What about standing grain? It is obligated in חלה!
phrases.notes: Dough made from this grain needs חלה taken off, so grain has something other crops don't.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the source from קמה just set up in steps 7-9.
steps.kashyaTarget: Learning the rule for all produce from קמה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: קמה has a unique obligation (חלה), so other produce may not share its law.

steps.title: Does the פסוק really mean grain that needs חלה
steps.stepSummary: A side question: how do we know the קמה in the פסוק is specifically grain obligated in חלה, and not any standing crop?
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we know that this standing grain is the kind that is obligated in חלה? Maybe the תורה means any standing crop!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses its main argument to ask a side question. Maybe the word קמה in the פסוק includes every standing crop, not just grain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If קמה meant any crop, the attack in step 10 would fall apart, because the פסוק would already cover everything. So the גמרא must first check what קמה means in this פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know?
Perhaps
'The Merciful One' — the Torah / ה׳

steps.confusionAlert: This is a side question. The גמרא is not dropping its challenge from step 10. It is checking a point first and will come back to that challenge in step 13.

phrases.english: And from where do we know that this standing grain
is standing grain that is obligated in חלה?
Perhaps the Torah is speaking about any standing crop!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִמַּאי דְּהַאי קָמָה קָמָה דְּמִתְחַיֶּיבֶת בְּחַלָּה הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side question about the assumption behind step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Proof that קמה in דברים 23:26 refers only to grain obligated in חלה.

steps.title: A גזירה שוה from the word קמה
steps.stepSummary: The word קמה also appears with the עומר harvest. Just as there it means grain obligated in חלה, so too here.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is learned from the same word, 'standing grain,' in two places. Here it says 'When you come into your neighbor's standing grain,' and there it says 'From when the sickle is first put to the standing grain.' Just as there it is grain that is obligated in חלה, here too it is grain that is obligated in חלה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the side question with a גזירה שוה, a matching word in two פסוקים. It proves that קמה here means only grain that needs חלה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same word appears in the פסוק about the worker and in the פסוק about counting from the עומר harvest. In the עומר פסוק the grain is clearly a חלה grain, so the word carries the same meaning in the worker's פסוק. So step 10's attack still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It comes' — it is learned from
Learning one פסוק from another through a matching word
Sickle
Here / there

phrases.english: It is learned from 'standing grain' and 'standing grain'
phrases.notes: The same word shows up in two פסוקים, so we learn one from the other.

phrases.english: It is written here: 'When you come into your neighbor's standing grain'
phrases.notes: דברים 23:26

phrases.english: and it is written there: 'From when the sickle is first put to the standing grain'
phrases.notes: דברים 16:9, about counting from the עומר harvest.

phrases.english: Just as there it is standing grain that is obligated in חלה,

phrases.aramaic: אַף הָכָא נָמֵי קָמָה דְּמִיחַיְּיבָא בְּחַלָּה.
phrases.english: so too here it is standing grain that is obligated in חלה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the side question of step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה between קמה in the worker's פסוק and קמה in the עומר פסוק shows it means grain obligated in חלה.

steps.title: Back to the challenge: grain has חלה
steps.stepSummary: With the side question settled, the גמרא repeats its challenge: קמה is special because of חלה.
steps.simpleTranslation: One can refute it: What about standing grain? It is obligated in חלה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the main problem from step 10 and states it again. This sets up a new way to solve it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 12 proved that the worker's קמה really is a חלה grain. So the challenge is now firm. Learning from קמה alone does not work, and learning from כרם alone did not work either (step 6).

keyTerms.meaning: 'One can refute' — there is a challenge to this proof
A refutation that shows a source is special

phrases.english: One can refute it:
What about standing grain? It is obligated in חלה!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the challenge of step 10 after the side discussion.
steps.kashyaTarget: Learning all produce from קמה alone.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: קמה is special because of חלה, so its law may not spread to other produce.

steps.title: The vineyard proves חלה is not the reason
steps.stepSummary: A כרם has no חלה, yet a worker may eat from it. So חלה is not what gives the right to eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let the vineyard prove it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the חלה challenge by pointing to the כרם. Grapes have no חלה, and a worker still eats from them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If חלה were the reason a worker may eat, a worker could not eat in a vineyard. Since he can, חלה is not the key feature.

keyTerms.meaning: Vineyard
Will prove
Exempt from חלה (as grapes are)

phrases.english: Let the vineyard prove it.
phrases.notes: Grapes don't need חלה, yet a worker may eat from them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 13.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe the worker's right to eat depends on the crop being a חלה grain.
steps.terutzMaskana: A כרם has no חלה and the worker still eats, so חלה is not the cause.

steps.title: The vineyard is special because of עוללות
steps.stepSummary: The vineyard can't serve as proof alone, because it has the special מצוה of עוללות.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about a vineyard? It is obligated in עוללות!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the vineyard proof. The vineyard has its own special feature, so it cannot be the source by itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This repeats the attack from step 6. Maybe עוללות is what gives a worker the right to eat in a vineyard.

keyTerms.meaning: Small undeveloped grape clusters that must be left for the poor
Obligated

phrases.english: What about a vineyard? It is obligated in עוללות!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof from כרם in step 14.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: כרם has a unique obligation (עוללות), so maybe that explains the worker's right.

steps.title: Grain proves עוללות is not the reason
steps.stepSummary: קמה has no עוללות, yet a worker eats from it. So עוללות is not what gives the right.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let standing grain prove it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by pointing back to קמה. Grain has no עוללות, and a worker may still eat from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each source knocks out the other's special feature. Grain shows עוללות is not the reason, and the vineyard showed חלה is not the reason.

keyTerms.meaning: Will prove (feminine form, for קמה)
Exempt from עוללות (as grain is)

phrases.english: Let standing grain prove it.
phrases.notes: Grain has no עוללות, yet a worker may eat from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Counter-example from the other source case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe the worker's right depends on עוללות.
steps.terutzMaskana: קמה has no עוללות and the worker still eats, so עוללות is not the cause.

steps.title: The shared feature of vineyard and grain applies to all produce
steps.stepSummary: Using הצד השוה, the גמרא concludes that anything that grows from the ground may be eaten by the worker when its work is finished.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reasoning has come back around. This case is not like that case, but what they share is that they grow from the ground and the worker eats when the work is finished. So too, anything that grows from the ground may be eaten by the worker when its work is finished.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא combines the vineyard and the grain. It takes only what they have in common and applies it to every crop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each source has its own special feature, but those features differ, so neither one can be the reason. What is left is what both share: they grow from the ground, and the worker eats at the end of the work. Every crop with those features gets the same law.

keyTerms.meaning: The reasoning has come back around
This case is not like that case
The common feature of two sources, used to learn a law
Things that grow from the ground
The finishing stage of the work
A hired worker

steps.whatToRemember: No single source works: כרם has עוללות and קמה has חלה. Together, with הצד השוה, they teach that a worker may eat from any produce that grows from the ground, at the time its work is finished.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the general הלכה of a worker's right to eat. It covers all crops, not just grapes and grain, and only at the finishing stage of the work.

phrases.english: The reasoning has come back around:
phrases.notes: Neither source works alone, so we go back and use both together.

phrases.english: This case is not like that case.
The common feature between them
is that each grows from the ground,

phrases.aramaic: וּבִשְׁעַת גְּמַר מְלָאכָה פּוֹעֵל אוֹכֵל בּוֹ.
phrases.english: and at the time the work is finished, the worker eats from it.
So too, anything that grows from the ground,

phrases.aramaic: בִּשְׁעַת גְּמַר מְלָאכָה פּוֹעֵל אוֹכֵל בּוֹ.
phrases.english: at the time the work is finished, the worker eats from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְחָזַר הַדִּין לֹא רְאִי זֶה כִּרְאִי זֶה הַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה שֶׁבָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Combines the back-and-forth of steps 13-16 into a final derivation.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Through הצד השוה of כרם and קמה, a worker may eat from all produce that grows from the ground, at the time its work is finished.

steps.title: Vineyard and grain share a link to the altar
steps.stepSummary: The הצד השוה is challenged: כרם and קמה both have a connection to the מזבח, so maybe only such produce is included.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about the common feature of these two? They both have a link to the altar.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the conclusion of step 17. It points out that grapes and grain share something special that other produce does not have.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A הצד השוה only works if the shared feature is the reason for the law. Grapes give wine for the נסכים, and grain gives flour for מנחות. So maybe the worker's right to eat comes from this altar link, and it does not cover all produce.

keyTerms.meaning: A connection to the altar, meaning the produce is offered on the מזבח
Since, because (it has a special feature)
What about...? The opening words used to break a proof

phrases.english: What about the common feature between them?
They have an aspect relating to the altar.
phrases.notes: Wine is poured on the altar as נסכים, and flour is brought in מנחות.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the הצד השוה conclusion of step 17
steps.kashyaTarget: The הצד השוה that extends the worker's right to all produce
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both sources share a link to the מזבח, so the derivation can only reach produce with that same link

steps.title: Then olives should be included too
steps.stepSummary: As a side point, the גמרא says olives would at least be included, since olive oil is also used on the מזבח.
steps.simpleTranslation: And olives should also be learned from this, since they too have a link to the altar.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא makes a side remark. Even with the new limit, olives should still be included, because their oil goes on the altar. This sets up the next question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the law covers only altar produce, the הצד השוה still reaches olives. Olive oil is used in מנחות. This is a small gain, not a full answer to step 18.

keyTerms.meaning: Olive
And let it also come (be learned)

phrases.english: And let an olive also be derived,
since it has an aspect relating to the altar!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side point that follows from the limit raised in step 18
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Olives, which have an altar link, would be included through the הצד השוה

steps.title: Why do olives need the common feature at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why olives need a הצד השוה, since a פסוק calls them כרם and they should already count as a vineyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do olives really come from the common feature? Olives themselves are called a vineyard, as it says: 'He burned the piles of grain, the standing grain, and the olive vineyard.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the side remark of step 19. It argues that olives are directly included in the word כרם, so no derivation is needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Torah's word כרם already includes olive trees, olives are covered by the vineyard פסוק itself. Then saying they 'come from the הצד השוה' is wrong. The proof is a פסוק in שופטים that uses the words כרם זית.

keyTerms.meaning: Is called
A pile of harvested grain
Olive vineyard, an olive grove

phrases.english: And does an olive come from the common feature?
It itself is called a vineyard,
as it is written: 'And he burned from the piles of grain
to the standing grain and the olive vineyard'!
phrases.notes: שופטים 15:5

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claim in step 19 that olives come from the הצד השוה
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that olives are derived through the הצד השוה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A פסוק calls olives כרם, so they are already included directly in the vineyard law

steps.title: An olive grove is not a plain vineyard
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that olives are called 'olive vineyard', but never just 'vineyard', so the Torah's plain כרם does not include them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: It is called 'olive vineyard', but it is not called just 'vineyard'.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא defends step 19. Olives still need the הצד השוה, because the plain word כרם does not include them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in שופטים adds the word זית to describe the grove. When the Torah says only כרם, it means grapes. So olives are not covered directly and must be learned from the הצד השוה.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who answers the question
Plain, without any added description

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
It is called 'olive vineyard',
but it is not called a plain 'vineyard'.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא כֶּרֶם זַיִת אִקְּרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 20
steps.terutzResolutionType: Precise reading of the פסוק's wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Olives are called כרם, so they are already included in the vineyard law
steps.terutzMaskana: Only 'olive vineyard' is used, not plain כרם, so olives must come from the הצד השוה

steps.title: The main difficulty still stands
steps.stepSummary: Leaving the olive side point, the גמרא says the challenge of step 18 is still unanswered.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, it is difficult!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the main question. Olives aside, there is still no source that the worker may eat from all produce.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The altar link of step 18 limits the הצד השוה to produce used on the מזבח. Produce like figs or dates would still not be included. So the search for a source must start again, and this sets up שמואל's answer.

keyTerms.meaning: In any case, either way
It is difficult; the question remains

steps.confusionAlert: 'It is difficult' points back to step 18, the altar question. It does not attack רב פפא's answer, which stands.

phrases.english: In any case, it is difficult!
phrases.notes: Olives aside, there is still no source for produce that is not used on the altar.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the olive branch and returns to the main challenge of step 18
steps.kashyaTarget: The הצד השוה as a source for all produce
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The altar link limits the derivation, so produce not used on the מזבח remains unsourced

steps.title: שמואל learns it from the word 'sickle'
steps.stepSummary: שמואל gives a new source: the word וחרמש in the פסוק includes everything that is harvested with a sickle.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, שמואל said: The פסוק says 'and a sickle' to include everything that is cut with a sickle.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the הצד השוה and brings a new source. שמואל reads the word חרמש as including all crops that are harvested.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about the worker mentions a sickle. שמואל says this word is there to widen the law to every kind of crop that is cut and harvested. This gives a source that does not depend on any altar link.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives the new source
Sickle, a tool for cutting crops
To include, to widen the law
Things that are harvested with a sickle

phrases.english: Rather, Shmuel said:
The verse says 'and a sickle'
phrases.notes: דברים 23:26

phrases.english: to include all things harvested with a sickle.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר קְרָא וְחֶרְמֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the difficulty of step 22 with a new source
steps.terutzResolutionType: New source from an extra word in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The source is the הצד השוה of כרם and קמה, which is limited to altar produce
steps.terutzMaskana: The word חרמש includes every crop that is harvested
steps.whyThisMatters: This moves the whole law onto a new source, so it no longer depends on the broken הצד השוה.

steps.title: The word 'sickle' is needed for timing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks that the word חרמש is already needed to teach that the worker eats only at harvest time.
steps.simpleTranslation: But this word 'sickle' is needed to teach: at the time of the sickle, eat; not at the time of the sickle, do not eat!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל's source. It says the word חרמש is already used for a different rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word חרמש teaches that the worker may eat only when the work is being finished, at harvest time. If the word is used for that rule, it cannot also be used to include all crops. So שמואל's source seems to be taken already.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed for something else
At the time of

phrases.english: But this word 'sickle' is needed for:
at the time of the sickle, eat,
phrases.notes: He means when the work is finished and the crop is being cut.

phrases.english: not at the time of the sickle, do not eat!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges שמואל's source in step 23
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's use of חרמש to include all crops
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word חרמש is already needed to teach that the worker eats only at harvest time, so it is not free for another teaching

steps.title: The timing rule comes from a different פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The rule that the worker eats only at harvest time is learned from 'ואל כליך לא תתן', so חרמש is free for שמואל's teaching.
steps.simpleTranslation: That rule comes from 'But you may not put any in your vessel.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge of step 24. The harvest-time rule has its own source, so the word חרמש is free to teach what שמואל said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 24 said the word חרמש is already used up by the timing rule. The answer moves the timing rule to a different phrase, 'ואל כליך לא תתן'. Now חרמש is left over, and שמואל can use it to include everything cut with a sickle.

keyTerms.meaning: That one (that rule)
Your vessel or container
It is learned from, it comes out of

phrases.aramaic: הָהוּא מִ״וְּאֶל כֶּלְיְךָ לֹא תִתֵּן״ נָפְקָא.
phrases.english: That rule is learned from 'But you may not put any in your vessel.'
phrases.notes: דברים 23:25. 'That rule' is the harvest-time rule from step 24; step 38 shows how the ברייתא learns it from these words.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא מִ״וְּאֶל כֶּלְיְךָ לֹא תִתֵּן״ נָפְקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 24
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves a competing teaching to a different source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: חרמש is needed for the harvest-time rule, so it cannot teach שמואל's rule
steps.terutzMaskana: The harvest-time rule comes from 'ואל כליך לא תתן', so חרמש is free for שמואל

steps.title: What about produce not cut with a sickle?
steps.stepSummary: חרמש covers produce harvested with a sickle, but what source includes produce that is not?
steps.simpleTranslation: This works for produce that is cut with a sickle. For produce not cut with a sickle, where do we learn it from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל's source. It only covers sickle-cut produce, and leaves out the rest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's word חרמש naturally covers only things harvested with a sickle. But the worker may also eat other kinds of produce, like fruit picked by hand. So חרמש cannot be the full source.

keyTerms.meaning: It works out well, that is fine
Something cut with a sickle
From where do we know?

phrases.english: It works out well for something cut with a sickle;
something not cut with a sickle, from where do we know it?

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּינַח דְּבַר חֶרְמֵשׁ, דְּלָאו בַּר חֶרְמֵשׁ מְנָא לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that חרמש is free, the גמרא shows it is too narrow
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The source is too narrow. It covers only sickle-cut produce, not all produce.

steps.title: רבי יצחק: the word קמה includes all standing produce
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק brings a new source. The word קמה includes anything that stands growing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי יצחק said: The פסוק says 'standing grain' to include everything that stands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops שמואל's source and brings a broader one from רבי יצחק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אלא shows the earlier approach is being replaced. קמה means standing crops in general, so it covers produce whether or not it is cut with a sickle.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (shows a new approach replacing the old one)
Standing grain or produce
To include
Things that have height, that stand

phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi Yitzchak said:
The verse says 'standing grain'
phrases.notes: דברים 23:26.

phrases.english: to include everything that stands.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק: אָמַר קְרָא ״קָמָה״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces שמואל's source after the challenge of step 26
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only sickle-cut produce is included through חרמש

steps.title: But קמה was limited to produce obligated in חלה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that earlier it read קמה narrowly, as grain obligated in חלה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But you said: 'Standing grain' means standing grain that is obligated in חלה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יצחק by pointing to how קמה was read earlier in the סוגיא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, קמה was one side of the הצד השוה, and it was read as only the five grains obligated in חלה. Now רבי יצחק reads the same word very broadly. The same word cannot mean both things.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't you say?
The portion of dough given to a כהן; only the five grains require it
Is obligated

phrases.english: But you said: 'standing grain'
means standing grain that is obligated in חלה!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יצחק's broad reading of קמה
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יצחק's broad reading of קמה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It contradicts the earlier narrow reading of the same word

steps.title: Once חרמש teaches, קמה is freed for a broad reading
steps.stepSummary: The narrow reading held only before חרמש was used. Now חרמש covers sickle-cut produce even without חלה, so קמה is free to include all standing produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: That was only before we brought in 'sickle.' Now that 'sickle' came, everything cut with a sickle is included, even if it is not obligated in חלה. So why do I need 'standing grain'? To include everything that stands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the earlier narrow reading of קמה no longer applies. Both words work together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, קמה had to carry the narrow job of grain obligated in חלה. Now חרמש already covers all sickle-cut produce, even produce without חלה, so קמה would be extra if read narrowly. Since it is extra, it is read broadly to include all standing produce, even what is not cut with a sickle.

keyTerms.meaning: These words apply (only in a certain case)
Is included
Why do I need it?

steps.whatToRemember: Final picture here: חרמש includes all sickle-cut produce, even without חלה, and קמה includes all standing produce, even without a sickle.
steps.confusionAlert: 'קמה למה לי' here is not a new challenge. It is part of the answer, showing that קמה is extra and so can be read broadly.

phrases.english: That applies before we bring in 'sickle';
now that 'sickle' has come,
everything cut with a sickle is included,

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא מִיחַיַּיב בְּחַלָּה.
phrases.english: even though it is not obligated in חלה.
Why do I need 'standing grain'?
To include everything that stands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 28
steps.terutzResolutionType: Earlier reading limited to before another source was used; extra word read broadly
steps.terutzHavaAmina: קמה means only grain obligated in חלה
steps.terutzMaskana: With חרמש in place, קמה is extra and includes all standing produce
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how the גמרא combines two words: once one covers part of the ground, the other becomes extra and widens the rule.

steps.title: Then why do we need the פסוק of the neighbor's vineyard?
steps.stepSummary: If חרמש and קמה already teach which produce the worker eats, the פסוק 'כי תבא בכרם רעך' seems unnecessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: And now that we learn it from 'sickle' and from 'standing grain,' why do I need 'When you come into your neighbor's vineyard'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new challenge. With two good sources in place, the vineyard פסוק looks extra.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the כרם פסוק was one of the two sides of the הצד השוה. Now that חרמש and קמה cover all produce, the כרם פסוק seems to add nothing. The גמרא wants to know what it teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: And now
Your neighbor's vineyard

phrases.english: And now that we learn it from 'sickle' and from 'standing grain,'
why do I need 'When you come into your neighbor's vineyard'?
phrases.notes: דברים 23:25.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַשְׁתָּא דְּנָפְקָא לַן מֵחֶרְמֵשׁ וּמִקָּמָה ״כִּי תָבֹא בְּכֶרֶם רֵעֶךָ״ לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the conclusion of step 29 to question the need for the כרם פסוק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It seems extra, since חרמש and קמה already cover all produce

steps.title: רבא: The verse is needed for its own special rules
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the פסוק 'כי תבא בכרם רעך' is needed for its own detailed rules. He begins with a ברייתא that uses a גזירה שוה on the word 'תבא' to show that the פסוק is about a hired worker.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: the פסוק is needed for its own rules. As a ברייתא teaches: 'When you come' uses the word 'coming,' and 'coming' is also used in another פסוק: 'the sun shall not set (תבוא) on it.' That other פסוק is about a worker, so this one is about a worker too.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the question from step 30. The פסוק is not extra, because it teaches its own set of rules, and the first rule is that it is talking about a hired worker.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חרמש and קמה teach which kinds of produce a worker may eat. The פסוק of כרם is still needed for the finer details of how he eats. The first detail comes from linking the word 'תבא' to the same word in the פסוק about paying a worker on time, which shows that 'כי תבא' means a worker who comes to do his job.

keyTerms.meaning: For its own rules: the פסוק is needed for its specific details
'Coming': the shared word that links the two פסוקים
A hired worker
'Just as there, so too here': the form of a גזירה שוה

steps.whyThisMatters: Without this link, someone could read 'כי תבא בכרם רעך' as letting anyone who walks into a vineyard eat from it. The גזירה שוה limits the permission to a worker.

phrases.english: Rava said: for its own laws.
phrases.notes: He means the פסוק isn't extra. It is needed for the details that come next.

phrases.english: As it is taught: "When you come",
"coming" is stated here,
and it is stated there:
"The sun shall not set upon it."
phrases.notes: דברים 24:15, about paying a worker the same day.

phrases.english: Just as there the verse speaks of a worker,
so too here the verse speaks of a worker.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 30, which asked why the כרם פסוק is needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows that the פסוק has its own purpose: detailed rules, not just which produce may be eaten.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The כרם פסוק seemed to repeat what חרמש and קמה already teach.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק is needed for its details, starting with the rule that it speaks of a hired worker.

steps.title: Your neighbor's vineyard, not a non-Jew's vineyard
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. The words 'בכרם רעך' teach that the rules of this פסוק apply to a Jew's vineyard and not to a non-Jew's vineyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'In your neighbor's vineyard,' and not in a non-Jew's vineyard.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא learns the next detail from the words 'your neighbor's vineyard.' This also sets up the question that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The restrictions on the worker, such as not putting grapes into his own vessel, apply only in a Jew's vineyard. In a non-Jew's vineyard the worker is allowed more, which is why the next step calls this 'permitting the worker.'

keyTerms.meaning: Your neighbor: here it means a fellow Jew
A non-Jew

phrases.english: "In your neighbor's vineyard,"
and not in a non-Jew's vineyard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the same ברייתא with the next phrase of the פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The worker's restrictions in this פסוק apply to a Jew's vineyard, not a non-Jew's vineyard.

steps.title: Why is a verse needed if stealing from a non-Jew is permitted?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the teaching of step 32 makes sense for the view that stealing from a non-Jew is forbidden. For the view that it is permitted, there is no need for a פסוק to permit a worker.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works for the one who says stealing from a non-Jew is forbidden, since then we need a פסוק to permit the worker. But for the one who says stealing from a non-Jew is permitted, if outright stealing is permitted, do we need a פסוק to permit a worker?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's reading 'and not a non-Jew's vineyard.' It works for one view but seems useless for the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If גזל נכרי is forbidden, a worker might also be held back in a non-Jew's vineyard, so the פסוק has to tell us he is allowed. But if even stealing from a non-Jew is permitted, then a worker taking grapes is obviously fine. A פסוק teaching that would be wasted.

keyTerms.meaning: Stealing from a non-Jew
'This works well for the one who says': opens a challenge against the other view
'Now': if the bigger thing is true, the smaller one surely is
'Is it needed?': it is obvious

phrases.english: This works well for the one who says
stealing from a non-Jew is forbidden;
that is why a verse is needed to permit a worker.
But for the one who says
stealing from a non-Jew is permitted,
now, if outright stealing is permitted,
is it necessary to say a worker is?!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנִיחָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר גֶּזֶל נׇכְרִי אָסוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the derivation in step 32 according to one view.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading 'בכרם רעך, ולא בכרם נכרי' according to the view that גזל נכרי is permitted.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: קל וחומר: if taking a non-Jew's property outright is allowed, a worker eating from it is surely allowed, so the פסוק teaches nothing new.

steps.title: That view reads it as excluding הקדש
steps.stepSummary: The one who permits גזל נכרי reads 'בכרם רעך' differently. It excludes a vineyard that belongs to הקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: He explains it this way: 'In your neighbor's vineyard,' and not one belonging to הקדש.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 33. The view that permits stealing from a non-Jew uses the words 'your neighbor's vineyard' to teach something else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For this view, 'your neighbor' excludes property of הקדש rather than a non-Jew's property. A worker in a הקדש vineyard may not eat from it. That way the words still teach something real.

keyTerms.meaning: He sets it up as: he reads the פסוק in a different way
Property belonging to the בית המקדש

phrases.english: He sets it up as:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the one who says stealing from a non-Jew is permitted.

phrases.english: "In your neighbor's vineyard" and not one of הקדש.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 33.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives a different reading of the same words for the other view.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'בכרם רעך' seemed useless for the view that גזל נכרי is permitted.
steps.terutzMaskana: For that view, 'רעך' excludes הקדש: a worker may not eat from a הקדש vineyard.

steps.title: Eat the grapes properly: no sucking, nothing added
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. 'ואכלת' means real eating, not sucking out the juice. 'ענבים' means grapes alone, not grapes eaten together with something else.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And you may eat,' but not suck. 'Grapes,' but not grapes together with something else.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the ברייתא and learns two more limits on how the worker eats.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worker must eat the whole grape. He may not suck out the juice and throw the rest away. He also may not eat the grapes with something else, such as bread or a dip, that would let him eat more of them.

keyTerms.meaning: Sucking out the juice
Grapes
Something else eaten together with the grapes

phrases.english: "And you may eat" but not suck.
"Grapes" but not grapes and something else.
phrases.notes: He means eating the grapes with another food that makes them easier to eat a lot of.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the side question about גזל נכרי to the ברייתא's word-by-word teachings.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The worker must eat the grapes normally. He may not suck the juice or eat the grapes with another food.

steps.title: The worker is exempt from מעשר just like the owner
steps.stepSummary: The word 'כנפשך' compares the worker to the owner. Just as the owner may eat a snack before the work is finished without taking מעשר, the worker may too.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Like yourself': like the owner himself, so is the worker himself. Just as you eat and are exempt, so too the worker eats and is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא learns its next detail from 'כנפשך.' The worker's eating is treated like the owner's eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An owner may eat produce before its processing is finished without separating מעשר. 'כנפשך' puts the worker in the same position, so he too may eat without separating מעשר. The ברייתא is not done yet; it learns two more rules from the rest of the פסוק in steps 37 and 38.

keyTerms.meaning: Like yourself: compares the worker to the owner
The owner of the field
Exempt: here, from separating מעשר

steps.whatToRemember: רבא's answer to step 30: the כרם פסוק is needed for its own details. It speaks of a worker; only a Jew's vineyard (or, for the other view, not הקדש); real eating, not sucking; grapes alone; and the worker is exempt from מעשר like the owner.

phrases.english: "Like yourself":
like the owner himself,
so is the worker himself.
Just as "yourself" eats and is exempt,
phrases.notes: Exempt from separating מעשר, since the produce isn't fully processed yet.

phrases.aramaic: אַף נַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁל פּוֹעֵל אוֹכֵל וּפָטוּר.
phrases.english: so too the worker himself eats and is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא's list of rules learned from the כרם פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A worker who eats from the produce, like the owner, is exempt from מעשר.

steps.title: Eat until full, but not excessive eating
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא learns from 'שבעך' that the worker may eat until he is satisfied, but he may not engage in אכילה גסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The word 'until you have enough' teaches that he may eat until he is full, but he may not stuff himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא keeps reading the פסוק one word at a time. Now it explains the word 'שבעך'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'שבעך' sets a limit on how much the worker may eat. He may eat until he is satisfied. Overeating, called אכילה גסה, is not included in his right.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'your fill': as much as satisfies you
Excessive eating, stuffing oneself past normal fullness

phrases.english: "Your fill" (until you have enough), but not excessive eating.
phrases.notes: Still the same פסוק, דברים 23:25.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא's word-by-word reading of the פסוק, after 'כנפשך' in step 36.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The worker may eat until he is satisfied, but not excessively.

steps.title: He eats only while filling the owner's baskets
steps.stepSummary: From 'ואל כליך לא תתן' the ברייתא learns that the worker may eat only while he is putting grapes into the בעל הבית's vessels, which means during the harvest.
steps.simpleTranslation: "But you may not put any in your vessel": when you are putting grapes into the owner's vessels, you may eat. When you are not putting grapes into the owner's vessels, you may not eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains the last part of the פסוק, 'do not put into your vessel'. It uses these words to set the time when the worker is allowed to eat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'your vessel' suggest a contrast with the owner's vessel. So the right to eat belongs to the time when the worker is filling the owner's baskets, which is the harvesting stage. Other work in the vineyard before the harvest does not give him this right.

keyTerms.meaning: Your vessel or container
The owner, the employer
At the time when

steps.confusionAlert: This is not only about forbidding the worker from taking grapes home in his own basket. The ברייתא also learns from these words when he may eat: only while he is harvesting into the owner's vessels.
steps.whatToRemember: The worker's right to eat comes with limits taken from the פסוק itself: real eating, grapes alone, until full but not excessive, and only while he is harvesting into the owner's vessels.

phrases.english: "But you may not put any in your vessel":
at a time when you are putting
grapes into the owner's vessel,
phrases.notes: The ברייתא is contrasting 'your vessel' in the פסוק with the owner's vessel. Filling his vessel means harvesting.

phrases.english: you may eat,
but at a time when you are not putting

phrases.aramaic: לְכֶלְיוֹ שֶׁל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת – אִי אַתָּה אוֹכֵל.
phrases.english: grapes into the owner's vessel, you may not eat.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״וְאַל כֶּלְיְךָ לֹא תִתֵּן״, בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאַתָּה נוֹתֵן לְכֶלְיוֹ שֶׁל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא's reading of the פסוק by explaining its final words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A worker may eat only during the stage of work when he is putting produce into the owner's vessels.

steps.title: רבי ינאי begins: when טבל becomes obligated in מעשר
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי begins a new teaching that טבל does not become obligated in מעשר until a certain point. The rest of the sentence continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ינאי says: Untithed produce does not become obligated in tithing...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new statement from רבי ינאי about when produce becomes obligated in מעשר. The sentence is cut off here and continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 36 said that a person may snack on produce before the work is finished without taking מעשר. רבי ינאי's statement deals with this same question of when the obligation of מעשר begins. The condition that completes his sentence comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Produce from which תרומות and מעשרות have not yet been taken
The tithe that must be separated from produce
Becomes obligated

phrases.english: Rabbi Yannai says:
untithed produce is not obligated in tithing

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יַנַּאי: אֵין הַטֶּבֶל מִתְחַיֵּיב בְּמַעֲשֵׂר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the ברייתא ends, the גמרא opens a new teaching about when the obligation of מעשר begins, the same subject raised in step 36.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: טבל is not yet obligated in מעשר until a condition that is stated on the next amud.
